newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian 1997 budget seen opening door to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Belgian 1997 budget seen opening door to EMU.

text.p: The Belgian 1997 budget, due next Tuesday, will be cobbled together with glue and string as usual, but should be convincing enough to open the door to European economic and monetary union, analysts said on Thursday.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's centre-left coalition has promised to cut the state deficit to below 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, from a targeted 3.0 percent in 1996.
Dehaene knows he must deliver, as early in 1998 the EU will look at the 1997 budgets of single currency candidates to determine who can join.
Dehaene has a formidable instrument to make sure he sticks to his promise: before summer, parliament agreed to allow the government to rule by executive decree until mid-August.

The so-called "framework laws" allow government decrees to take immediate force of law without parliamentary approval. If unexpected events threathen his budget, Dehaene can revise his budget immediately -- a luxury no other European leader has.
"I am convinced the 1997 deficit will be cut to 3.0, even 2.9 percent," said Generale Bank chief economist Peter Praet, adding that he was sure Dehaene would keep his budget on track.
"That is why markets are so positive about Belgium."
Belgian 10 year bonds yielded 6.22 percent on Thursday, a historically low 15 basis points over equivalent German bonds.
But like most of his colleagues, Praet has doubts about the quality of the budget package.
As in all previous budgets of the past decade, the 1997 one is expected to be full of minor spending cuts and tax hikes, complemented by one-shot measures and some accounting tricks.
A serious reform of Belgium's generous welfare system -- the root of all budget evil -- is not expected this year.
"Belgium is not made for revolutions, and the budget will be typically Belgian: a series of little cuts," said Credit Communal economist Jacques De Pover.
Analysts estimate the government will need to take between 100 and 110 billion francs ($3.51 billion) worth of austerity measures.
About 30 billion is seen coming from social security, partly from an increase in women's retirement age to 65 from 60.

A hike of indirect taxes is seen providing another 30 billion francs. Labour income in Belgium is already taxed to the hilt, but Belgium's indirect taxes only add up to 12.4 percent of GDP in 1995, compared to 13.6 percent for its three big neigbour states and 13.4 percent for the EU, a BBL study said.
"There is room for a hike," said BBL's Kristin Vandenbergen.
Recent newspaper leaks spoke of higher excise duties on beer and spirits and a two-franc per litre increase in petrol taxes.
The financial sector is also expected to contribute about 10 billion francs with a "turnover tax" on regulated savings accounts and a tax on physical delivery of securities.
Among the expected one-shot measures, the most likely is a further privatisation of ASLK-CGER bank.

The central bank is also chipping in. A recent renewal of 100 franc-notes is expected to leave five to 10 billion worth of old bills in socks and under mattresses -- an easy gain which the bank can pass on to the treasury.
The bank is also expected to chop a major chunk off Belgium's 9,828 billion franc debt mountain -- at a forecast 131.8 percent of GDP the highest in the EU.
Tonnes of gold sold in recent years have left the central bank with 236 billion francs worth of foreign exchange in its accounts, booked as capital gains on the liability side.
The harmonisation of central bank accounting rules in the single currency project is an opportunity to use this hoard to buy back part of Belgium's 970 billion franc foreign debt.
($1=31.34 Belgian Franc)
